lesson.title: What Is a Number?
lesson.summary: Introduces the idea of a number as an abstract quantity that can count, measure, or label ,  the basic object that all of algebra manipulates.
lesson.body:
Before you can do algebra, you need to be clear about what you're actually working with, and the answer is: numbers. A number is not a mark on a page ,  that mark is just a symbol, called a numeral, that stands for the number. The number itself is the underlying idea of "how much" or "how many" that the symbol represents. When you write 5, you're using a numeral to point to the number five, which is really an abstract answer to a question like "how many apples are in this basket?"

Numbers show up because people needed to solve different kinds of problems, and each kind of problem pushed the idea of "number" a little further. Counting whole things ,  apples, coins, days ,  gives you numbers like 1, 2, 3. But counting alone can't tell you how much liquid is in a jug if the amount falls between two whole units, so measuring calls for numbers like 2.7, which sits between 2 and 3 and captures a fractional amount precisely. Owing money, or tracking temperature below zero, calls for negative numbers like -3, since "less than nothing" needs a way to be represented too. And some quantities that show up naturally in the real world, like the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter (written as the number π), or the length of the diagonal of a square with side length 1 (which is √2), turn out not to be expressible as a simple ratio of whole numbers at all ,  yet they are still perfectly definite quantities, so they still count as numbers.

Here's a concrete way to see how these different needs connect. Suppose you have a square garden bed with sides exactly 1 meter long, and you want to know how long a diagonal path across it would be. That length is a real, measurable distance ,  you could get close to it with a tape measure ,  but no matter how you try to write it as a fraction, you can't land on it exactly; it works out to √2, approximately 1.41421. That number wasn't invented to make math harder; it's the honest answer to a measuring question, and it forces you to accept that "number" has to include more than just whole counts and neat fractions.

What makes all of this fit under one umbrella called "number" is that every one of these objects ,  5, -3, 2.7, π, √2 ,  can be placed on a single number line, compared in size, added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided using the same basic rules. That shared behavior is exactly why algebra can treat them uniformly: an equation or a formula doesn't need to know whether a number came from counting sheep, measuring a board, or computing a ratio. It only needs the number to behave like a number ,  to have a definite size and to combine with other numbers in predictable ways.

As you move forward, you'll meet more precise categories within this broad idea ,  ways of sorting numbers by how they arise and how they behave ,  but every one of those categories will still be answering the same basic question this section raised: what quantity, exactly, does this symbol represent?
